html:
Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi was a mathematician, astronomer and geographer of the 9th century, active at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, capital of the Abbasid Caliphate. His family name points to Khwarazm, the oasis land on the lower Oxus river in Central Asia.

Little is known of his life. He worked around 820 under the caliph al-Mamun, who gathered scholars to translate and extend Greek, Persian and Indian learning.

His two most famous books:

  • A short book on calculation by "completion and balancing", written between 813 and 833. It solved linear and quadratic equations step by step, with geometric proofs, and treated algebra as a subject of its own. The word algebra comes from al-jabr in its title.
  • A book on calculating with the Indian numerals, the decimal system with a zero that had just reached Baghdad. Its Latin translation in the 12th century began "Algoritmi said...", and his name became our word algorithm.

He also drew up astronomical tables and revised the world geography of Ptolemy.

Through Latin translations, his books taught Europe the Hindu-Arabic numerals and the methods of algebra. That is why a man from Khwarazm stands on this chart in Central Asia: his learning came from Baghdad, but his name travelled to every school in the world.
